title: The boy who brought the rain
hook: a forest boy welcomes strangers as guests and the rain follows him; why Hindus treat the guest as God
carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is God
tomorrow: why did Ravana never fear a human?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's sacrifice begins, and your line: yajna, bringing what you lack to the sacred fire. Sumantra remembered a prophecy.

Deep in a forest lives a sage, Vibhandaka, and his son, Rishyashringa. The boy has grown up with only his father, the trees, the sacred fire and the animals. He has never been to a town, never seen anyone but his father. Meanwhile, in the kingdom of Anga, a long way off, the rain has stopped. Fields crack. Wells sink. The king, Romapada, asks his priests what to do, and they give him an odd answer: bring the forest boy here, and the rain will come with him.
screen: `A BOY WHO'S ONLY SEEN HIS FATHER.` → `A KINGDOM WITHOUT RAIN.` → `BRING THE FOREST BOY.`

segments.voice: Here's how Sumantra tells it. The king's people can't march in and take a sage's son. So they send young women from the city into the forest, with sweets and garlands. Rishyashringa, who has never met anyone, thinks they're young hermits from another ashram, and welcomes them the way a host should: water, a seat, roots and fruit. They give him sweets he takes for a new kind of fruit, and invite him to their hermitage. It's a gentle trick, but no one lays a hand on him. He goes with them, all the way to Anga, and the moment he enters the kingdom, the rain pours down. The king honors him and gives him his daughter, Shanta, in marriage. Dasharatha hears this, goes himself to Anga, to his old friend Romapada, and brings Rishyashringa and Shanta home to Ayodhya with great honor. Then, on the bank of the Sarayu, the horse is released to wander for a year before the great rite. Look at how everyone behaves in this story. The forest boy receives strangers as honored guests. The king of Anga invites him and gives him a family. Dasharatha travels in person to bring the sage home. It's hospitality all the way down, and Hinduism makes that a teaching: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you, a line from the Taittiriya Upanishad. That's why a Hindu grandmother won't let you leave without eating, why guests are served first, why many temples feed whoever comes. And in this story, where the guest is honored, the sky answers.
screen: `THE KINGDOM OF ANGA, WITHOUT RAIN.` · `HE WELCOMES STRANGERS AS GUESTS.` · `WHERE HE GOES, RAIN FOLLOWS.` · `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA.` · then, large: `THE GUEST IS GOD.`

segments.voice: Rishyashringa met strangers the way a host meets guests, with water, fruit and an open door. Let each breath arrive like a guest, welcomed without pulling it in, and see each one off kindly. If you pray, picture one person you'll host or meet this week, and silently welcome them as you would God.
Dasharatha's sacrifice. To perform it, the king brings Rishyashringa, the forest sage whose coming brought rain to a dry kingdom, to Ayodhya.
Your line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is God. A dry kingdom, and one honored guest. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Rishyashringa is honored at some local temples in India, and his story is told as part of the Ramayana's opening, as the reason the rain-bringing sage leads Dasharatha's rites.

original.note: Sanskrit ṛśyaśṛṅga: deer-horned, from ṛśya, a kind of antelope, and śṛṅga, horn.

trapdoor: what you thought: a side story before the real one starts.
what it means: it shows who the sage is, someone the sky answers, and a chain of honored guests: atithi devo bhava.

what a scholar hears: the Rishyashringa episode is also told in the Mahabharata's Vana Parva; in Valmiki's southern recension Shanta is Romapada's daughter, while some later tellings make her Dasharatha's daughter adopted by Romapada.
